title: International Diversification: Developed and Emerging Markets
content:
Many retail investors fall victim to 'home country bias'—the psychological tendency to allocate the overwhelming majority of their portfolios to domestic companies. For US investors, while the US equity market represents roughly 60% of total world market capitalization, investing solely in domestic equities ignores 40% of global corporate enterprise and economic opportunity.

Global equities are divided into Developed Markets and Emerging Markets. Developed markets—such as Japan, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Canada—feature stable regulatory environments, mature economies, robust rule of law, and established corporate governance. Emerging markets—such as India, Brazil, Mexico, and Taiwan—feature younger demographic profiles, rapid urbanization, and higher economic GDP growth trajectories, though accompanied by political, currency, and regulatory volatility.

Allocating capital internationally offers critical diversification benefits. Different national economies experience distinct business cycles, monetary policies, and sector concentrations. For instance, European indices offer higher weightings in industrials, luxury goods, and healthcare, whereas the US is technology-heavy.

Furthermore, international investing introduces currency exposure. If the US Dollar weakens relative to the Euro, Japanese Yen, or British Pound, foreign investment returns convert into higher dollar-denominated gains for domestic investors. Financial institutions like Vanguard generally recommend allocating between 20% and 40% of an equity portfolio to international assets using broad low-cost index funds like VXUS or IXUS.
